findings.title: Findings are discarded four ways: non-blocking AI review findings never leave the process, and the gate-refusal deduper that already exists is never called
findings.body:
Found by rg-findings-audit during a read-only inventory of the finding lifecycle. Filed now because it is independent of any design question about what to build next — it is data being discarded today.

## Four places a finding dies

### 1. Non-blocking AI review findings are parsed, held in memory, and dropped at process exit

`AI_REVIEW_SEVERITIES` (`lib/scaffold/ai-review-step.ts:2086`) marks `medium`, `low` and `info` as non-blocking. On a CLEAN reading, `aiReviewRefusal()` returns `null` and the `detail[]` array is populated only for blocking findings.

So a reviewer that writes ten `medium` findings produces: a green check, an `adjudicated: CLEAN` notice, and **no emitted text at all**. The findings were parsed into `reading.reported`, held in memory, and lost when the process exited.

This is the sharpest of the four, because the data was **fully structured and then discarded**. Everything else on this list is lossy; this one is total.

### 2. Blocking findings survive only as a capped annotation

The payload is written to `${RUNNER_TEMP}/ai-review-findings-<nonce>.d/ai-review-findings.json`, deliberately outside the checkout — and `RUNNER_TEMP` is destroyed with the job. No workflow uploads it: grepping for the upload/download artifact actions across all eight workflows yields exactly one hit, `suite-flake.yml:60`. `ai-review.yml` has no artifact upload, no PR comment, no issue creation.

What escapes is one `::error title=AI review findings::` annotation, each finding rendered through `renderFinding()` and **capped at 300 characters** (`AI_REVIEW_DETAIL_MAX`), joined with `; `. That is subject to log retention, is not queryable, and cannot be deduplicated.

**The `::notice title=AI review adjudicated::` added by #1087 does not change this.** It carries the outcome word only, lifted from the outcome line. It is a liveness proof for the adjudicator — the one annotation an unread payload cannot produce — and was never intended as evidence retention. Worth stating explicitly so nobody reads that issue as having solved this.

### 3. Gate refusals are durable, and the deduper that reads them is never called

`~/.rungate/<repo>-<issue>/workflow-state.json` accumulates gate failure entries with timestamps. Measured against the live store on 2026-10-22: **44 run stores, 28 carrying refusals, 111 refusal entries across 19 distinct check names**, top check appearing 22 times across 18 runs. This is the richest durable finding data the harness holds.

`lib/intake-sources.ts` already dedupes exactly this: by check name, keeping the newest citation, counting occurrences across runs, refusing UNMEASURED rather than returning an empty list when the store is unreadable. Its docblock gives the right reason — one candidate per entry would give 111 dominated by repeats against a promotion budget of 16; one per distinct check gives 19, and **the repetition becomes evidence rather than noise**.

Verified against `origin/main`: `mineGateRefusals` and `INTAKE_SOURCES` are referenced by exactly two files — their own module and `test/intake-sources.test.ts`. **Written, tested, reading data that is on disk right now, and nothing in production calls it.**

What is wired instead is the weaker half: `lib/conformity.ts:2244` (HYGIENE-6) calls `extractConstraints`, which uses the git-log source only, never the aggregate. It prints and asserts nothing. On CI the checkout action runs with no fetch-depth and clones to depth 1, so it reports `UNMEASURED/SHALLOW_HISTORY` on every runner.

### 4. Incidental agent findings have no mechanism at all

Nothing in `.claude/` logs a finding. `~/.rungate/hook-firings.jsonl` records hook decisions, not findings. The only durable route today is a human telling an agent to file one.

`.claude/routines/post-merge-conformity.md` instructs opening an issue on conformity regression — but **routines have no runner.** Grepping `routines` outside `.claude/routines/` yields a CODE-MAP line and `test/routines.test.ts`, which validates the markdown's trigger syntax only. No lib, script, hook, bin or workflow executes them.

`AgentVerdictCapture.hook.ts` appends agent-reported blockers to a `verifyBlockers` array, deduped by id — the only dedupe-on-write in the repo. That key is **absent from all 44 live stores**. It has never fired.

## What a fix must not duplicate

- `lib/intake-sources.ts` + `lib/failure-intake.ts` + `lib/rule-promotion.ts` — dedupe-by-key, occurrence counting, UNMEASURED-vs-empty discipline, evidence-gated promotion with eviction at 16. **Wire it; do not rewrite it.**
- `~/.rungate/compliance-history.jsonl` + `lib/compliance-report.ts` — append-only JSONL, versioned schema, verdict carrying evidence *and the rule text as it read at grading time*. 390 entries, 2026-09-25 to 2026-10-21. The store-format question is already answered; #116 fixed the lossiness.
- `.github/workflows/issue-audit.yml` — the scheduled-job-reads-state-and-writes-to-the-tracker pattern. It exists because a predict-from-the-command hook kept being wrong and the control was moved to reading the outcome instead. That is the precedent.
- The four ratchets (ai-review-surface, conformity-allowlists, config-access, line-citation) are **allowlists, not dedupe stores** — each names a known-exempt state keyed on its subject, and records nothing about when or how often a finding was seen. Do not build a fifth for that shape.

## Suggested smallest first step

Persist the full findings payload on every ai-review run, including CLEAN. That closes loss 1 entirely and most of loss 2, needs no new store design, and is a precondition for any dedupe. Whether it goes to an artifact, the tracker, or `~/.rungate` is the open question.

## Caveats from the audit

- GitHub Actions log and annotation retention for this org was **not** verified; "retention-limited" is the platform default, asserted not measured.
- `gates/orchestrator.ts` and `gates/run-gate.ts` internals were not read, so which gate paths write failure entries is unknown.
- `lib/rule-health-pipeline.ts`, `lib/rule-health-trend.ts`, `lib/instruction-effectiveness.ts`, `lib/rule-registry.ts`, `lib/rule-retirement.ts`, `lib/promote-outputs.ts` and `lib/hill-climb.ts` were not opened. There may be more wiring — or more dead wiring — in them.

Related: #1155 (gate-enforcement fails open on unparseable state — a second reader of the same files), #1161 (SC-453 ticked without an implementation).

---

**Criteria served** (CODE-REVIEW-CONVERGENCE-SPEC.md, mapped in `docs/adr/ADR-003-increment-1-issue-plan.md`): CRC-B8 — every finding is answered, never silently dropped. The same defect as "findings are discarded four ways", stated from the spec's side.

findings.title: PROTECTED_FILES matches by basename with no notion of tree: 144 of 234 newly-blocked commands are agents writing legitimate /tmp test fixtures
findings.body:
`PROTECTED_FILES` in the Bash write guard matches by **basename**, with no notion of which tree a path is in. Measured on a 5,060-command real corpus during #1120: of 234 commands the hardened guard newly blocks, **144 are interpreter writes to `workflow-state.json` under `mkdtemp` or `/tmp`.**

Every one of those 144 is a **true positive against the rule as written** and a **false positive against intent**. They are test fixtures. An agent building a fixture for the very guard that refuses it is doing exactly the right thing and getting stopped.

## Why this is now a design gap rather than a deferral

`specs/HOOK-ARCHITECTURE-SPEC.md` already defers the same question for the `*.hook.ts` arm. It now bites a second arm. **A deferral that recurs in a second place is a design gap**, and the enumerate-by-basename approach is what both arms inherit.

The 144 is also an understatement of the friction: it counts one corpus on one machine. Every consumer writing a fixture named `workflow-state.json` anywhere on disk inherits the same refusal, and they will not have the corpus to discover why.

## Why it was not fixed inside #1120

Scoping to the project root makes every guard decision depend on correctly resolving that root. That dependency was **broken until today**: #1129 was exactly this failure — `nonCanonicalRoots()` compared a canonicalised path against an un-`resolve()`d root, and a root spelled with a trailing slash or a `.` segment broke containment in ship.js's `collectDestination`, measured at **5 of 6 spellings**. The production fix merged as `1e4f1b57`; the test lock-in is **#1165**.

Building root-relative protection on top of root resolution that stabilised the same day is the wrong order. That is the only reason this is a separate issue and not part of #1145.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A protected artifact is identified by its path **relative to the project root**, not by basename
- [ ] A write to a same-named file outside the project root is allowed, and there is a witness case for it
- [ ] A write to the real artifact is still refused, including when the root is spelled non-canonically — reuse `resolve()`-then-compare from #1129 rather than writing a second copy
- [ ] An **unresolvable** root refuses rather than allows. This is the fail-open risk the change introduces and it must be a named case, not an implicit default
- [ ] Re-run the 5,060-command corpus: the 144 go to allowed, and the count of newly-blocked **real** writes does not drop

## Predict before measuring

State an integer for how many of the 234 clear, and a case list, before re-running the corpus. The expected answer is 144, which makes this a good calibration: a result that is not 144 means either the scoping is wrong or the original count was.

## Dependency

**#1165** — the #1129 lock-in tests — should land first, so the canonicalisation this relies on cannot silently regress underneath it.

Found during #1120. Reported by the implementing agent as explicitly out of scope and handed up rather than taken quietly, which was the right call.

findings.title: `lib/bash-write-guard.ts` has six parser-differential bypasses: the view each check reads differs from what the shell executes
findings.body:
Shipped in #1145 (merged `fbc37e62`). All six are the same class — a check reads a *transformed* view of the command (heredoc-stripped, quote-stripped, segment-split) and the transformation loses or relocates the very token the check is looking for. Found by a background commit review; seven claims were relayed, I predicted six real before measuring and measured six.

Predicted ALLOWED: 6 of 7 — F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7. Measured: identical, same case list.

## The six

Each case uses a throwaway path under `/tmp/bw/`. Protected basenames are written here as prose; in the regression tests they are assembled at runtime so the literal never appears in a Bash command line (the installed hook refuses its own test fixtures otherwise).

### F1 — HIGH — `stripHeredocs` eats the rest of the operator's line

`stripHeredocs` is `/<<-?\s*(['"]?)([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\1[\s\S]*?^\s*\2\s*$/gm`. The lazy body starts immediately after the delimiter word, so it consumes everything after `<<EOF` on that line — including a redirect.

```
input:  cat <<EOF > /tmp/bw/<SALT>
        hello
        EOF
output: "cat  "
```

`writeTargets` never sees the redirect. **Allowed.** Fix: strip only the lines *between* the operator's line and the terminator; keep the operator's own line intact. Secondary: the regex has no quote-state awareness, so `echo "<<EOF"` plus any later bare `EOF` line strips across unrelated code — recognise `<<WORD` only at top level.

### F2 — HIGH — redirect targets are read off the VERB view

`writeTargets` runs the redirect regex over `stripQuoted(segment)`, which deletes quoted spans *and their contents*. A second pass at the `:175` recovery line recovers a target that is **wholly** quoted. A target with a quote in the middle of the word is matched by neither.

- `> "dir"/<STATE>` — still blocks. stripQuoted leaves `/<STATE>`, which carries the basename. The claim as originally relayed is wrong on this case.
- `> dir/"<STATE>"` — **allowed**. The recovery pass requires the quote to directly follow `>`.

Fix: derive targets from `dequote(stripHeredocs(segment))` and consume the whole word, `((?:[^\s'"]|'[^']*'|"[^"]*")+)`, dropping the two-pass approach entirely.

### F3 — HIGH — `tee` takes one operand

`code.match(/\btee\s+(?:-a\s+)?(\S+)/)` — no `/g`, one capture group. `tee` accepts many files.

```
writeTargets("tee /tmp/a /tmp/bw/<STATE>")  ->  ["/tmp/a"]
```

**Allowed.** Fix: collect every non-option operand.

### F4 — HIGH — the gate-salt check reads `stripQuoted`

The real invocation quotes the key name, and `stripQuoted` deletes it:

```
security find-generic-password -s '<SALTKEY>'   ->  allowed
```

The check therefore cannot fire on the actual command shape it exists to catch. Fix: decide per segment — block when `commandWord(seg) === 'security'` **and** `dequote(seg)` names the key. This preserves the two real false positives that motivated reading code-not-prose (issue bodies quoting the command they propose to guard), because their command word is `gh`. Verify that rather than assume it.

### F6 — MEDIUM — `2>` is not treated as a write sink

The lookbehind `(?<![2&])` excludes `2` and `&`.

```
echo x 2> /tmp/bw/<SALT>   ->  writeTargets []  ->  allowed
```

`2> <file>` truncates just as hard as `> <file>`. **Narrower than originally claimed:** `3> /tmp/bw/<SALT>` captures the target and blocks, so this is not "every `N>`" — the live hole is `2>` alone. Fix: drop `2` from the lookbehind; keep `/dev/null` and `/dev/stderr` exempt; skip the duplication form where the operand matches `&?\d+` or `-`.

### F7 — HIGH — a shell `-c` body is scanned for *program* write idioms

`isInterpreter` is `INTERPRETERS.test(word) && /\s-[a-z]*[ce]\b/.test(code)`, and the body is then matched against `WRITE_INTENT`, which enumerates Node/Python idioms (`writeFileSync`, `.write(`, `open(...,'w')`, `shutil.*`). For `sh`, `bash`, `zsh`, `dash`, `ksh` the body is **shell**, so a plain redirect is invisible:

```
bash -c 'echo x > /tmp/bw/<SALT>'   ->  allowed
```

Arm 1 cannot see it either, because `stripQuoted` deleted the quoted body. Both arms miss it for different reasons, which is why it survived. Fix: for those five command words, recurse `decideBashWrite(dequote(body))`. Also extend `WRITE_INTENT` with shell idioms (`>`, `>>`, `tee`, `rm`, `mv`, `cp`, `dd of=`, `truncate`) so a non-shell interpreter that shells out still fires.

## One claim that is NOT real

### F5 — `segments()` splitting `&>` — NOT A DEFECT

Claimed: splitting on a bare `&` cuts `&>` in half and the operand lands in a segment with no operator. Measured, the split *closes* the hole rather than opening it:

```
segments("echo x &> /tmp/bw/<SALT>")  ->  ["echo x", "> /tmp/bw/<SALT>"]
writeTargets("> /tmp/bw/<SALT>")      ->  ["/tmp/bw/<SALT>"]   ->  BLOCKED
```

In the second segment the `>` is no longer preceded by `&`, so the lookbehind passes. This is the module docblock's stated design — "over-splitting costs precision in the allow direction and never opens a hole" — holding in practice.

Worth recording why it was reported: `&>` **was** a real bypass in the round-1 revision `cfadf934`, where there was no segmentation and the whole command string hit the lookbehind at `hooks/BashWriteGuard.hook.ts:81`. The rewrite dissolved it. Two separate reviews reported it against line numbers that no longer exist in the merged 60-line hook.

## Acceptance

- A regression test per real case, each proved red against `fbc37e62` before the fix.
- A negative control: the existing 12 allow-cases must stay green, including the recorded `pai-config#474` false positive.
- F1 and F7 interact — once F1 keeps the operator's line, the heredoc case grows a redirect for arm 1 — so sweep the 5,060-command corpus with all six applied **together** and report one before/after, not six.
- Report newly-blocked and newly-allowed counts against `origin/main` as the baseline (B0 = 258 blocked on the pre-#1145 code; current main is the new baseline and must be re-measured).

## Not in scope

- `install` and the `cp -p src /x/<STATE>` destination case — #1146.
- Scoping `PROTECTED_FILES` to the project root — filed separately; depends on #1165.

findings.title: `PROTECTED_FILES` matches by basename, so BashWriteGuard refuses 144 legitimate test fixtures under `/tmp` and `mkdtemp`
findings.body:
## The measurement

Sweeping 5,060 unique real commands (extracted from 35,040 transcripts on this machine) through `lib/bash-write-guard.ts` as merged in #1145:

| Reading | Count |
|---|---|
| newly blocked vs the pre-#1145 guard | 234 |
| of those, interpreter writes to a gate-artifact basename under `/tmp` or `mkdtemp` | **144** |

Those 144 are **true positives against the rule as written** and false positives against intent. They are agents writing `workflow-state.json` fixtures into a scratch directory — exactly the right thing to do — and being refused because the guard matches a basename with no notion of which tree it is in.

`PROTECTED_FILES` is `['workflow-state.json', '.gate-salt', '/witnesses/']`, tested with `String.includes` against a resolved-ish target string. A fixture at `/var/folders/.../T/rg-abc123/workflow-state.json` matches as readily as the real one at the project root.

## Why this is not a quick fix, and why it should not ride along with a guard patch

1. **Blast radius is the whole guard, not one arm.** Basename matching is what lets the guard work with zero configuration in any consumer repo. Replacing it with root-relative matching makes *every* decision depend on correctly resolving the project root, in a PreToolUse hook that must also decide correctly when the root cannot be resolved at all.

2. **That dependency stabilised only on 2026-10-22.** #1129 was precisely this failure: `nonCanonicalRoots()` compared a canonicalised path against an un-`resolve()`d root, so a root spelled with a trailing slash or a `.` segment broke containment in `collectDestination` — measured, 5 of 6 spellings. The fix landed as `1e4f1b57`; **the test lock-in is #1165 and is still open.** Building root-scoped protection on top of root resolution that has no regression test yet is the wrong order.

3. **The 144 deserve their own number.** A false-positive class with a measured denominator (234 newly blocked, 5,060 swept) is the strongest kind of issue to prioritise, and folding it into a bypass fix would bury it.

## This is no longer a deferral — it is a design gap

`specs/HOOK-ARCHITECTURE-SPEC.md` already defers exactly this question for the `*.hook.ts` arm: *"The `*.hook.ts` arm is still unscoped … settle that before `deployToConsumers`."* It now bites a second arm, in a different mechanism, with a measured cost.

A deferral that recurs in an arm nobody wrote it for is not a deferral any more; it is an unstated design decision — "protected names are global" — that was never chosen, only inherited. The spec note should be promoted from a per-arm caveat to a module-level decision, resolved either way and written down.

## Options, not a recommendation

- **Scope to the project root.** Clears all 144. Requires the guard to resolve a root, and to decide what to do when it cannot — refusing on UNMEASURED is defensible for a guard but changes behaviour in every unscaffolded tree.
- **Exempt well-known scratch prefixes** (`/tmp`, `/var/folders`, `mkdtemp` results, `TMPDIR`). Cheaper and needs no root, but it is an allowlist — and #1120's whole finding was that the previous allowlist had six of eleven entries with no recorded justification.
- **Do nothing and document it.** The 144 are refusals of real work; agents route around a guard that does this, which is the failure mode `WRITE_INTENT`'s docblock already warns about.

## Depends on

- #1165 — regression lock-in for the root-resolution fix `1e4f1b57`. Should land first if the scoping option is chosen.

## Context

- #1120 / PR #1145 — the rework that produced the measurement.
- `.claude/rules/checks-must-be-able-to-fail.md` — "a guard tuned so wide that people work around it protects nothing".

findings.title: Five more guard bypasses, one of them a regression #1182 introduced: unterminated heredoc, herestring, quoted verb, directory destination, and case-insensitive paths
findings.body:
Follow-up to #1176 / PR #1182. Five findings confirmed by running them; a sixth was relayed and **does not reproduce**, recorded below so nobody re-files it.

All cases use throwaway paths under `/tmp/bw/`. Protected basenames are assembled at runtime in the tests so the literal never appears in a Bash command line.

## H1 — HIGH — an unterminated heredoc deletes every later line. **This is a regression #1182 introduced.**

`stripHeredocs` was rewritten in #1182 from a terminator-anchored regex to a line scanner. The scanner runs off the end when the terminator never appears:

```js
while (i < lines.length && lines[i].trim() !== delim) i++;
```

Nothing is pushed to `out` for those lines, so they vanish.

```
input:  cat <<EOF
        echo x > /tmp/bw/<SALT>
stripHeredocs -> "cat <<EOF"          decision -> ALLOW
```

The old regex required `^\s*\2\s*$` to match, so an unterminated heredoc produced **no match and no strip** — it failed closed. The replacement fails open. This is strictly worse than what it replaced and is reachable with one unterminated heredoc.

**Fix:** buffer the skipped lines; if the scan reaches `lines.length` without matching the terminator, emit them **unchanged**.

This is the one finding here that the corpus sweep could not have caught — an over-strip looks exactly like a clean parse, and the #1182 sweep reported `R = 0` because no real command in 5,516 had an unterminated heredoc.

## H5 — HIGH — a `<<<` herestring is misread as a heredoc

`heredocDelimiter` is `/<<-?\s*(['"]?)([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\1/`, which matches inside `<<<` by starting at the second `<`:

```
grep x <<< "t"          ->  delimiter "t"
```

A herestring is not a heredoc and has no terminator, so this lands directly in H1 and eats the rest of the command:

```
grep x <<< "t"
echo y > /tmp/bw/<SALT>        ->  ALLOW
```

**Fix:** exclude `<<<`, and only recognise `<<WORD` at a redirect position. Belongs with H1 — it is the same code path and the same failure.

## H3 — HIGH — the VERB is read off the view the attacker controls

The mirror of #1176's F2. There, redirect *targets* were read off the quote-stripped view; here the *verb* is. `commandWord()` resolves its token from `stripQuoted(segment)`, and both `IN_PLACE` and the interpreter test match against `code`, which is also quote-stripped. Quoting the command word therefore changes what the guard thinks is running while the shell runs it unchanged:

```
commandWord('"chmod" 777 x.hook.ts')   ->  "777"
```

```
"chmod" 777 /tmp/bw/hooks/X.hook.ts         ->  ALLOW
ch"mod" 777 /tmp/bw/hooks/X.hook.ts         ->  ALLOW
"bash" -c 'echo x > /tmp/bw/<SALT>'         ->  ALLOW
```

**Fix:** resolve the verb from a **dequoted** token stream after wrapper and assignment stripping, and strip a leading `(`, `{` or `\` from the first token. Keep `stripQuoted` only where it earns its place — the measured grep-PATTERN false positive it was introduced for.

## H4 — HIGH — a directory destination is never resolved to its real sink

`writeTargets` takes the last non-option argument of `cp`/`mv`/`install`/`rsync` and tests that string. When the destination is a directory the real sink is `join(dest, basename(src))`:

```
cp /tmp/forged/<STATE> /Users/jhorn/.rungate/x/    ->  ALLOW   (writes x/<STATE>)
mv /tmp/forged/<STATE> /Users/jhorn/.rungate/x/    ->  ALLOW
cp /tmp/evil/X.hook.ts …/rungate/hooks/            ->  ALLOW
```

`writeTargets` returns `["/Users/jhorn/.rungate/x/"]`, which names no protected artifact.

**Fix:** when the destination ends in `/` or is an existing directory, test `join(dest, basename(src))` for **every** source operand.

**Not taking the second half of this finding as relayed.** It also proposed testing every non-option operand, which would block `cp /x/<STATE> /tmp/backup.json` — reading a protected file and copying it *out*. That is not a write to the protected artifact and blocking it is a new false-positive class against exactly the backup-and-inspect work agents do constantly. If it should be blocked, that is a confidentiality argument, not an integrity one, and belongs in its own issue with its own measurement.

**Overlap with #1146:** `install` and the `cp -p` destination case live there. The destination-directory resolution is taken **here**, because it is the same line of code as the existing `cp`/`mv` handling and splitting it would leave two issues editing one expression. #1146 keeps `install` as a *verb* addition and the `-p` flag parsing.

## H6 — HIGH — protected names are matched case-sensitively on a case-insensitive filesystem

Measured on this machine before writing anything:

```
lower inode=582291290  upper inode=582291290
SAME FILE — case-INsensitive filesystem
```

So `WORKFLOW-STATE.JSON` and `workflow-state.json` are the same file here, and both guards miss the uppercase spelling:

```
echo x > /tmp/bw/WORKFLOW-STATE.JSON        ->  ALLOW
echo x > /tmp/bw/.GATE-SALT                 ->  ALLOW
cp /tmp/evil.ts /tmp/bw/hooks/X.HOOK.TS     ->  ALLOW
```

This spans two modules — `names()` in `lib/bash-write-guard.ts` uses `text.includes(p)`, and `isWorkflowState()` in `lib/gate-result-protection.ts` uses `filePath.endsWith('workflow-state.json')`.

**The severity is platform-dependent and the original finding did not say so.** On a case-sensitive filesystem these are different files and there is nothing to bypass. The fix is still correct everywhere — a case-insensitive match over-blocks only a file that cannot exist alongside the real one on the platform where it matters — but **the test must state which world it asserts**, and assert the platform fact rather than assuming it.

## H2 — relayed, NOT reproduced. Do not re-file without a witness.

Claim: blanking a `#` line in `stripHeredocs` drops that line's quote characters and desyncs quote state downstream, because a `#` inside a quoted span is not a comment.

The mechanism is real — the line *is* blanked wholesale. No bypass was found in five attempts:

```
echo 'text\n#quoted\n' > /tmp/bw/<SALT>                          -> BLOCK
python3 -c 'import os\n# it"s fine\nopen("/tmp/bw/<SALT>","w")…' -> BLOCK
bash -c "echo a\n# don't\necho x > /tmp/bw/<SALT>"               -> BLOCK
# a " quote\necho x > /tmp/bw/<SALT>                             -> BLOCK
```

The reason is directional: blanking removes an **unbalanced** quote, which makes the downstream balance more correct, not less, and the write stays visible. The desync fails toward blocking. Not fixing it — adding a quote-preserving blanker would be complexity with no witness. **If someone finds a witness, reopen with the command.**

## Acceptance

- A red case per confirmed finding, proved red against `6ddc587e` before any fix. H1 and H5 must be red as *over-strip* assertions on `stripHeredocs` directly, since a decision-level test alone cannot distinguish an over-strip from a clean parse.
- The existing #1120 and #1176 populations stay green, including the recorded `pai-config#474` false positive.
- One before/after corpus sweep with all fixes applied together, with the instrument control planted first — a sweep returning zero and a dead sweep return the same number.
- Predict the sweep integer before running it.

findings.title: Nothing arbitrates whether a finding is worth filing: 14 filed / 6 closed per hour, and the dedupe machinery that exists is pointed at rules instead of findings
findings.body:
Nothing judges whether a finding is worth filing. Every finding an agent produces becomes an issue, and the swarm files faster than it closes: measured at 15:24 today, **14 filed / 6 closed in one hour** against 27 open.

This is the gap named in #1166's description of the source post — *"several agents hunt, a separate group votes, a finding posts only on agreement"* — but the quorum is **not** the right first implementation here, and the reason is measured.

## What actually went wrong with filing today

Four real filing failures from one session. A correctness vote catches **none** of them:

| failure | what happened | would a vote catch it? |
|---|---|---|
| duplicate | #1175 and #1177 filed 5 min apart — same defect, same 5,060-command corpus, two agents | **No.** Both are real. Every voter says "real." |
| wrong branch | 9 of 10 findings in one day were about unmerged peer branches, not `main` | **No.** The finding is true of the tree the reviewer read. |
| stale citation | findings cited `hooks/BashWriteGuard.hook.ts:81` and `:115` in a **60-line** file — a superseded revision, and for one of them the fix direction was *inverted* | **No.** Voters read the same stale text. |
| unmeasured remedy | two suggested widenings died on corpus measurement: one predicted 900 newly-blocked and measured **2,101**; the other measured **100 newly-blocked against 4**, because `>{1,2}\s*\S` matches `=>` | **No.** Plausible to every reader. Only a corpus kills it. |

A vote answers *"is this real?"*. Our failures were *"is this new?"*, *"is this here?"*, *"is this current?"*, *"does the remedy work?"* — all mechanically decidable by one agent, and none decidable by agreement.

The source post's own number says the same thing: on the >50-round PR, `git blame` showed **~59% of repeat flags were on code present at the first pass** (recorded in #1168). That is a staleness-and-dedupe failure wearing a correctness costume.

## Proposed shape: a gate in cost order, not a jury

Each stage only runs on what survives the one before it, so the expensive instrument is never spent on what a `git grep` can settle.

**Stage 1 — mechanical, no model.**
- Dedupe on a key derived from the *measured symptom* (file + symbol + reading), not the issue title. #1175/#1177 have near-identical measurements and completely different titles; a title-keyed deduper would have missed them.
- Branch scope: does the cited symbol exist on `origin/main`? If it only exists on an unmerged branch, it is a comment on that PR, not an issue.
- Citation currency: does the cited line exist in the current file? `wc -l` is the whole check and it caught the `:81`-in-a-60-line-file case before any investigation was spent.

**Stage 2 — evidence gate.**
A finding carries a command that fails today and passes after the proposed fix, or it is UNMEASURED. Keep the existing doctrine: **UNMEASURED must FAIL, never skip.** This is the stage that would have killed both refuted widenings, and it is the one with the best measured track record here — the strongest result of the session was a prediction of 6-of-7 real, stated as an integer *and a case list* before measuring, that matched exactly on both.

**Stage 3 — vote, and only here.**
Reserve agreement for what survives 1 and 2 and still cannot be settled by measurement — the judgment calls. #1166's case is the archetype: a blocking finding with a fabricated `failure_scenario`, no `file` and no `line` adjudicates **identically** to one with real evidence. No mechanical check separates those two; a second opinion is the only instrument left.

## Do not rewrite what exists

`lib/intake-sources.ts` (380 lines), `lib/failure-intake.ts` (323) and `lib/rule-promotion.ts` (234) already implement dedupe-by-key, occurrence counting, ranking, evidence-gated promotion and a hard cap (`PROMOTION_BUDGET_RULES = 16`). The machinery is live and correct — it is pointed at **which rules get promoted into agent context**, not at **which findings become issues**. Same shape, different subject.

Wire it to the filing boundary. Do not build a second one. This is the same instruction #1162 gives for its own fix.

## Why this is not blocked the way the quorum is

`ai-review.yml:841` passes `--disallowedTools Bash,…,Task,…`, so the reviewing agent cannot spawn anything and cannot convene a quorum inside CI (#1166). **The filing boundary has no such constraint** — it runs in the orchestrating session, outside that sandbox. So stages 1 and 2 are available today without reversing a tool denial that four separate causes are recorded against in `lib/review-tool-agreement.ts`.

## Precision over recall, deliberately

The source post states its priority as "catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second." That is correct when a human absorbs the noise — a person waves off a nit in seconds. **Nobody waves anything off here.** A false finding costs a remedy commit, a CI round, a review round, and an agent's full context. #1169 makes this argument for the reviewer; it applies with more force at filing, where the artifact persists.

## Acceptance

- A finding that duplicates an open issue's *measurement* is not filed, and the existing issue gets an occurrence count instead.
- A finding whose cited symbol is absent from `origin/main` is not filed as an issue.
- A finding whose cited line exceeds the file's length is not filed without re-reading.
- A finding with no failing command is recorded UNMEASURED and does not become an issue.
- The gate can fail: plant a known-good finding and a known-duplicate finding and show the gate separates them. A filter that passes everything and a filter that works are indistinguishable without this (`.claude/rules/checks-must-be-able-to-fail.md`).
- Nothing in `lib/intake-sources.ts`, `lib/failure-intake.ts` or `lib/rule-promotion.ts` is duplicated.

Related: #1162 (findings discarded four ways — the opposite end of the same lifecycle), #1166 (payload contract unenforced), #1168 (nothing bounds review rounds), #1169 (no negative control, noise unmeasured).

findings.title: PR #1188 introduced two guard defects, measured on merged main: an assignment prefix flips 3 of 10 blocked writes to allowed, and cp/mv decisions depend on filesystem state
findings.body:
Two defects introduced by PR #1188 (`fb072926`, merged 15:48) and confirmed on `origin/main` after the merge. Both were posted on the PR before it merged; the merge raced the review (see the coordination note at the end).

#1188 is a net improvement — it closes H1, H3, H4, H5 and the case-folding hole. These two are the cost, and they are cheap to pay back.

All rows below were produced by calling `decideBashWrite` directly from a throwaway worktree at `origin/main`.

## 1. HIGH — `commandWord` resolves the wrong verb through an assignment prefix

`commandWord` now reads `dequote(stripHeredocs(segment))`. That is the right *direction* — it is what fixes H3, where `stripQuoted` deleted `"chmod"` outright and `'"chmod" 777 x.hook.ts'` resolved to `777`. But `dequote` keeps the bytes, so a quoted multi-word assignment value survives `split(/\s+/)`, and the `tok.includes('=')` skip drops only its first token:

```
plain                           word=rm
"ch"+"mod" quoted verb          word=chmod     <- H3, fixed
FOO=bar rm -rf …                word=rm
FOO="x grep" rm -rf …           word=grep      <- wrong
A="1 cat"   rm -rf …            word=cat       <- wrong
```

**A corrupted verb is not automatically a bypass, so the question measured was whether any decision changes.** Ten write commands, each run bare and again prefixed with `A="1 grep" `:

| | bare | prefixed | command |
|---|---|---|---|
| | blocked | blocked | `rm -rf <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `sed -i '' s/a/b/ <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `echo x > <protected>` |
| **FLIP** | blocked | **allowed** | `cp /tmp/forged/workflow-state.json <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `tee <protected>` |
| **FLIP** | blocked | **allowed** | `chmod 777 …/hooks/x.hook.ts` |
| **FLIP** | blocked | **allowed** | `mv /tmp/a <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `truncate -s 0 <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `dd of=<protected>` |
| | allowed | allowed | `python3 -c "open('<protected>','w')"` |

**3 of 10 flip from blocked to allowed on merged main.** The three are `cp`, `mv` and the hook `chmod` — the copying verbs #1188 extends, and hook integrity. The seven that hold are redirect-driven and never consult the command word, which is what makes them a control rather than padding. The last row is not a regression: an interpreter write is allowed on both sides, which is the shape #1146 covers.

**Net effect on the hook `chmod` case is a wash, not a win.** Before #1188, `"chmod" 777 x.hook.ts` was allowed (H3). After, that spelling is caught and `A="1 grep" chmod 777 x.hook.ts` is allowed instead. Worth stating plainly so the H3 fix is not recorded as closing the hook-integrity hole.

**Suggested direction — measure it, do not take it.** Tokenise quote-aware rather than dequoting then splitting: walk the segment with `readWord`, which already keeps `X=a b` as one word, and apply the existing skip rules per whole word. The cheaper variant worth running as the control is: drop any token whose predecessor contained `=` before whitespace. Run the 5,521-command sweep both ways and compare the newly-blocked **case list**, not the count — two proposed widenings on this file have already died on corpus measurement this week, one of them measuring 2,101 against a predicted 900.

## 2. MEDIUM — `isDirDestination` makes the decision from filesystem state

```
TOCTOU  dir-present=true   dir-absent=false   mkdir&&cp=false   slash-control=true
```

Identical command, identical protected source basename (`/tmp/forged/workflow-state.json`); the only variable is whether the destination exists when the hook runs.

`slash-control=true` isolates the cause: the trailing-slash path works, so it is `statSync` and nothing else.

**`mkdir&&cp=false` is the row that matters operationally.** `mkdir -p d && cp <protected> d` is a single Bash call and the hook runs before any of it, so the destination never exists at decision time. That is not a race anyone has to win — it is the ordinary way an agent creates a fixture directory.

A security decision that depends on local filesystem state also means the same command is allowed on one machine and refused on another, which makes any corpus sweep over it non-reproducible.

**Suggested fix:** always push `dest/basename(src)` for every non-last argument **in addition to** `dest`, and delete `isDirDestination` and the `statSync` import. The plain-file reading is already covered by pushing `dest`, so the extra candidates only over-block when a *source* basename is itself a protected artifact name — precisely the case worth refusing. Expected newly-blocked count is small; produce the case list.

**Not covered either way, and not measured:** a recursive copy. `cp -r /tmp/forged/ <protected-dir>/` pushes `dest/forged`, never `dest/forged/workflow-state.json`. Recorded as an observation, not a confirmed finding.

## Acceptance

- The ten-row bare-vs-prefixed table above runs as a test and reports **0 flips**.
- The four TOCTOU readings are a test, and `dir-present` and `dir-absent` agree.
- `statSync` is absent from `lib/bash-write-guard.ts`.
- The mutation control holds: revert the fix and the new rows go red. A row that cannot go red is not evidence (`.claude/rules/checks-must-be-able-to-fail.md`).
- Assertions are on `commandWord` and `writeTargets` **directly**, not only through `decideBashWrite` — #1184 established why for `stripHeredocs`, and the same argument applies: a wrong verb and a right verb can produce the same decision, so a decision-level test can be true and uninformative.

## Coordination note — why this merged with an open review on it

Auto-merge on #1188 was **disarmed** so the two findings could be addressed first. The author, independently, had earlier run `gh pr merge --auto` through `tail -2`, lost the output, and could not confirm it armed. On re-checking they found `autoMergeRequest: NONE`, read that as their own arming having silently failed, re-armed, and the PR merged.

**A disarm by the lead and a failed arm by the author produce the identical observation.** Neither party did anything wrong with the information they had. Two fixes, both cheap: a disarm should leave a PR comment saying so and why, and an arm should be confirmed by reading `autoMergeRequest` rather than by the command's exit. Filed here rather than as its own issue because it is one sentence of process, not a code change.

Related: #1184 (the five bypasses #1188 fixes, plus H6 posted there), #1146 (interpreter writes, the last row of the table), #1175 (`PROTECTED_FILES` basename scoping).

findings.title: Two regressions #1188 shipped to main, plus H6: `<<WORD` inside a quoted span drops the lines after it
findings.body:
#1188 merged at 15:48:31Z (`fb072926`) before auto-merge could be disarmed, so **both regressions below are live on `main` now**. One of them reopens hook integrity. Reproduced by executing `origin/main`'s own code; every row below is labelled witness or control.

## R1 — HIGH — a quoted multi-word assignment prefix hides the verb. **Regression from #1188.**

#1188 changed `commandWord` to read `dequote(stripHeredocs(segment))`. `dequote` strips the quote characters but keeps the bytes, so a quoted assignment VALUE survives the whitespace split as separate tokens — and only the first of them carries the `=` that the skip looks for.

```
commandWord('A="1 grep" cp /tmp/forged/<STATE> /x/<STATE>')  ->  "grep"
```

```
WITNESS  A="1 grep" cp /tmp/forged/<STATE> <protected>   ALLOW
WITNESS  A="1 grep" mv /tmp/forged/<STATE> <protected>   ALLOW
WITNESS  A="1 grep" chmod 777 <hook>                     ALLOW
CONTROL  cp /tmp/forged/<STATE> <protected>              BLOCK
CONTROL  chmod 777 <hook>                                BLOCK
CONTROL  echo x > <protected>                            BLOCK
```

The three that flip are the copying verbs and the hook mode change — exactly the arms that consult the command word. The redirect control blocks because it never consults it, which is what makes these controls rather than filler.

**The H3 fix in #1184 was right; this spelling of it is wrong.** Dequoting the whole segment and then splitting on whitespace is not tokenisation. The fix is to tokenise quote-aware so a quoted span stays *inside* its word — `A="1 grep"` becomes the single token `A=1 grep`, which contains `=` and is skipped. `readWord` in the same module already does exactly this and should be the one tokeniser.

## R2 — HIGH — the decision depends on filesystem state at decision time. **Regression from #1188.**

`isDirDestination` calls `statSync`. Same command, same protected source basename, only the destination's existence differs:

```
cp /tmp/forged/<STATE> /tmp/bwprot-dir
  dir ABSENT   ALLOW
  dir PRESENT  BLOCK
  with a trailing slash, no stat needed   BLOCK
```

The trailing-slash row isolates `statSync` as the cause.

**This is not a race anyone has to win.** A PreToolUse hook decides before the whole command runs, so in `mkdir -p d && cp <protected> d` the directory never exists at decision time and the write is always allowed.

**Fix:** delete `isDirDestination` and the `statSync` import; always push `dest/basename(src)` for every non-last operand *in addition to* `dest`.

One cost to measure rather than assume: that also blocks `cp /x/<STATE> /tmp/backup.json` — copying a protected file *out* — which #1184 deliberately allowed and has a control for. Whether that control survives is a corpus question, not an argument, and the sweep must report the case list.

## H6 — HIGH — `<<WORD` inside a quoted span is read as a heredoc operator

Not a regression; it predates #1184 and #1188 and is **not** covered by either.

```
bun -e 'x = "<<EOF"'
rm -rf <protected>
EOF
```

```
WITNESS  ALLOW   (the scanner receives only: bun -e 'x = "<<EOF"')
CONTROL  BLOCK   (same two lines, no heredoc operator — so multi-line input is not the cause)
```

Measured on both trees: the unterminated row flipped false→true with #1188's H1 fix, the terminated row is unchanged. So #1188 fixed the unterminated half and left this one.

This sits between H1 and H5: **H5 is `<<WORD` matching at the wrong character position; H6 is `<<WORD` matching at the wrong quoting position.** Both then fall into the same body-drop.

**The fix is not the one #1176 already refused.** Restricting to "not inside quotes" reddens the recorded `pai-config#474` false positive, whose heredoc is legitimately nested inside `"$(cat <<'EOF' … )"`. What distinguishes them is command substitution: `$(` opens a fresh command context in which quoting resets. A bounded `$(`/`)` stack over the existing quote scan tells the two apart without becoming a shell parser — it expands nothing and tracks no other construct. Both cases must be asserted.

## Acceptance

- A red case per finding against `fb072926` before any fix, each labelled witness or control.
- The recorded `pai-config#474` false positive and the #1120 / #1176 / #1184 populations stay green.
- H6 cannot be measured by corpus alone — an over-strip looks exactly like a clean parse, so `R = 0` is consistent with "nothing does this" and with "the detector is blind." Plant the rows first and show the instrument control.
- One before/after sweep with all three applied, predicted before it is run, with the case list for R2's cost.
- Production churn under ~500 lines.

findings.title: The adjudicator pin has no publish-pending tolerance, but distribution-standing does — every version bump blocks every open PR
findings.body:
Found by #1221 happening, and it will happen again on the next bump.

## The asymmetry

Two checks read the same state — *the tree is at version N, the registry serves N−1* — and they disagree about whether it is legal.

- **`distribution-standing` tolerates it by design.** `SUCCESS.md`'s standing line reads `tree 0.8.1, published rungate@0.8.0` and the check is **green**. #1049 built that tolerance deliberately: `distributionViolations` compares the standing line to `package.json` and to the registry **independently**, which is what makes a release a two-commit operation instead of an atomic one nobody can perform.
- **The adjudicator pin has no equivalent.** `.github/workflows/ai-review.yml` runs `bunx rungate@<generating version>`, so between the bump merging and the publish landing, the command cannot resolve. Since #1180 that fails closed — correctly, since an adjudicator that did not run has measured nothing.

`ai-review` is a **required** context on `main`. So a state one mechanism was deliberately built to accept is a state another turns into a repo-wide merge block, for every open pull request, for the length of the publish.

## This is not an argument for re-pinning

`lib/scaffold/ai-review-step.ts` documents the pin's behaviour as designed, and the reasoning holds:

> The version is the GENERATING version… A tree whose version is not yet on the registry emits a command that cannot resolve, and that is the same correct-but-not-yet-resolvable output `harnessDevDepRange` in `lib/scaffold/steps.ts` has emitted since #364.

Three reasons a hand re-pin to the published version is worse than the problem: the workflow is **generated**, so the edit reverts on the next regeneration; the security rationale for `bunx <pkg>@<generating version>` is precisely that it *"names its version in the generated file, so it cannot drift without the file changing"*, and pinning below the tree breaks that invariant on purpose; and it would adjudicate an N tree with N−1's adjudicator.

**The precedent the docstring cites does not carry the weight it is being asked to.** `harnessDevDepRange` emits the same unresolvable-for-now output, but nothing required gates on it. `ai-review` does. The analogy is sound about the *output* and silent about the *consequence*, which is the whole difference.

## Measured, from the one instance we have

- Window: bump merged 18:48:45Z, registry served 0.8.1 at roughly 19:05Z — **about 16 minutes**, most of it the full suite the release runs against the tag before publishing.
- Nine open pull requests were `BLOCKED` across it.
- The blast radius **grows** rather than holding steady: PRs that passed did so because their merge ref predated the bump (#1218 was created 45 seconds before it), and that protection expires as merge refs recompute.
- Clearing it was **not automatic**. A required check that has already failed does not re-run when the external condition resolves, and auto-merge does not retry it — #1220, #1208 and #1202 each needed a manual re-run after the publish.

That last point is the one that makes this more than a 16-minute annoyance: without someone watching, those PRs sit armed over a red check indefinitely.

## Options, unranked — this needs a decision, not a patch

1. **Give the pin the same publish-pending tolerance the standing line has.** When the pinned version is unresolvable *and* the tree's `package.json` names that same version, report a distinct state — `RELEASE_PENDING` — rather than the generic UNMEASURED refusal. The risk to weigh: it is a new path that returns something other than red, and this repository's recurring defect is exactly that shape. It would need a case proving it cannot be reached when the version is merely wrong rather than merely unpublished.
2. **Make the window not exist.** Publish from the bump PR's own merge, or move the pin in a follow-up commit after the publish, so the tree never carries a pin to a version that does not exist. Costs the invariant that the pin always equals the generating version — and #1013 chose that invariant deliberately, so this is a reversal to make consciously.
3. **Leave it and document it.** Add the sequence to a release runbook: expect every open PR to go red, re-run `ai-review` on each after the publish. Cheapest, and it is a manual step that will be forgotten exactly once.

My read is that (1) is right and (3) is the honest interim, but I have not measured anything that decides between them — and whoever takes this should say which of the five SUCCESS.md claims it moves before building, because it is possible the answer is none and this is cleanup with a loud symptom.

Related: #1221 (the instance), #1180 (the fail-closed that makes it blocking), #1013 (why the pin is the generating version), #1049 (the tolerance that exists on the other side), #1207 (the override label, which is the current escape hatch and has three defects of its own).

## Criteria this serves

CRC-M15

findings.title: Write-guard bypass: an escaped quote inside $( ) swallows the redirect operator — ALLOWed, and the executed command overwrote the file
findings.body:
An escaped quote inside a `$( )` substitution desynchronises the word scanner in `lib/bash-write-guard.ts`, the redirect operator is swallowed with the rest of the word, and the write is ALLOWed. **Executed: the file was overwritten.**

The substitution scanner skips quoted spans with `indexOf`:

```ts
const q = s[j];
if (q === "'" || q === '"') {
  const close = s.indexOf(q, j + 1);
  j = close === -1 ? s.length : close;
  continue;
}
```

`indexOf` cannot tell `"` from `\"`, so inside a double-quoted span the escaped quote is read as the closing one.

## Measured, with controls, on `origin/main`

`decideBashWrite()` against a protected basename:

| spelling | decision |
|---|---|
| `echo hi > <protected>` | BLOCK (control) |
| `chmod 777 <protected>` | BLOCK (control) |
| `echo $(echo "x)") > <protected>` | BLOCK (control — the paren-in-string case, already fixed) |
| `echo $(echo 'x)') > <protected>` | BLOCK (control) |
| `echo \$(echo x) > <protected>` | BLOCK (control) |
| **`echo $(echo "x\"") > <protected>`** | **ALLOW** |
| **`echo $(echo "a\")b") > <protected>`** | **ALLOW** |

Five blocking controls, so this is a reading and not a dead instrument.

## And they run

The whole argument for treating the unterminated spellings as acceptable is that they are not valid bash. That defence does not reach these two. Executed against a real file seeded with `ORIGINAL`:

```
  *** WROTE   rc=0  plain redirect (control)   victim now: hi
  *** WROTE   rc=0  escaped dq in $()          victim now: x\"
  *** WROTE   rc=0  escaped dq then paren      victim now: a\"\)b
  INERT       rc=2  unterminated dq            bash: unexpected EOF
  INERT       rc=2  unterminated $(            bash: unexpected EOF
```

Two of the four ALLOWed spellings are valid bash that exits 0 and overwrites the target. The other two are syntax errors and are genuinely inert — **that half of the automated review's finding does not hold, and I am not asking for it to be fixed.**

## Not introduced by #1213, and it should not block it

I ran the identical battery against #1213's head (`origin/pr-1213`) and against `origin/main`. Both ALLOW both escape rows. #1213 neither causes nor fixes this, and it does fix the paren-in-string case that was live when I first measured it — so #1213 is a strict improvement and I have left its auto-merge armed.

One incidental difference, no behavioural cost: main BLOCKs `echo $(echo "x) > <protected>` and #1213's head ALLOWs it. Both are rc=2 syntax errors, so neither decision reaches a real write.

## Fix direction

Make the substitution scanner a character walk that honours `\` and the single/double-quote asymmetry (single quotes take no escapes; `\"` escapes inside double quotes), rather than `indexOf`.

**Do not reach for the fail-closed-on-unterminated change in the same commit.** It is the tempting addition and the measurement above says it buys nothing: the only spellings that reach that branch do not run. Shipping it alongside the real fix would make the regression test green for two reasons and leave nobody able to say which one held.

Acceptance rows, both expected red first:

- `echo $(echo "x\"") > <protected>` → BLOCK
- `echo $(echo "a\")b") > <protected>` → BLOCK
- and keep the five blocking controls above, or the battery cannot show the fix did anything.

Worth sweeping the corpus for real incidence as #1203/#1205 were — both of those measured 0, and a verb list built from the histogram was worth more than the filed shapes.

SUCCESS.md claim moved: 3 — the harness's own checks are able to fail. This one cannot, today, against a command that runs.

findings.title: The scratch exemption: a protected tree is subtracted under one spelling only, and the exemption reaches an arm whose premise forbids it
findings.body:
Three findings from the 2026-10-22 security review of #1197, all against code I wrote in #1175 and all now on `main` (`430a1dc6`). Routed to me rather than filed; filing the pair that needs a decision, because one of them **reverses behaviour #1175 shipped** and that is not mine to decide alone.

Finding 1 is fixed in the PR that references this issue. Findings 2 and 3 are the decision.

---

## 1 — `protectedTrees()` resolved but never realpathed. FIXED in the PR.

`resolve()` normalises `.` and `..`; it does not follow a symlink. `scratchRoots()` already recorded both spellings for the fixed roots, so the asymmetry sat inside one file: the roots a write may land in were realpathed and the trees it may not were not.

Executed against `origin/main`'s module with `RUNGATE_WORK_DIR=/tmp/e2e`:

```
isScratchPath=false blocked=true    /tmp/e2e/s/workflow-state.json          the spelling anyone types
isScratchPath=true  blocked=false   /private/tmp/e2e/s/workflow-state.json  ← the run store, ALLOWED
```

Identical for `RUNGATE_HOOKS_DIR`. `/tmp` is a symlink to `/private/tmp` on every macOS install, so the second spelling is not exotic — it is what `realpath` prints. After the fix all four rows block.

**The corpus is blind to this one: newly blocked 0, newly allowed 0 over 5,586 commands.** It has to be, because the sweep runs under an environment whose protected trees are not symlinked. Only a unit test that builds a symlinked tree can measure it, which is what the PR adds — the same shape as the `tmpdir()` realpath gap #1175 hit earlier.

## 2 — The scratch exemption reaches arm 3, where the destination is not on the command line. DECISION NEEDED.

Arm 3's premise is that the program is **opaque**: it refuses because what an interpreter writes cannot be read off the command line. The exemption contradicts that premise by deciding the destination from a path word on the command line. Measured against `main`, one of three computed spellings escapes:

```
BLOCK  literal run-store path in a -e body        (control)
ALLOW  literal /tmp fixture in a -e body          (control)
BLOCK  computed with ..                           resolve() normalises it back into the store
ALLOW  "/tmp/x/workflow-state.json".replace("/tmp/x", "<run store>")   ← escapes
BLOCK  os.path.join with .. components
```

Enumerating `+`, `%`, `.replace`, f-strings and `..` is a detector narrower than what it detects (`.claude/rules/checks-must-be-able-to-fail.md`). Two options were built and swept rather than argued about:

| | closes the escape | answers the objection | corpus cost | #1175 witnesses broken |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **drop the exemption from arm 3** | yes | yes — no list at all | **12** | **2 of 10** |
| exempt only if EVERY absolute literal in the body is scratch | yes | no — still reads literals | **6** | 0 |
| leave it | no | — | 0 | 0 |

**Why this needs a decision rather than a fix.** #1175's central witness table is ten write shapes, each asserted to be a fixture under a scratch root and refused under a live one. Dropping the exemption reverses two of the ten — `python3 -I -c "… open('<scratch>/p/workflow-state.json','w')"` and `bun -e 'writeFileSync("<scratch>/p/workflow-state.json", …)'` — and those two rows went red when I implemented it. The 12 corpus commands are the same class: agents building gate fixtures in `/tmp` with `bun -e` or `python3 -c`, which is the workflow #1175 existed to unblock.

Worth knowing before deciding: **one of the twelve opens with the comment** *"The Bash hook blocks writing workflow-state.json. Let me use bun -e to create it"* — so at least one is the arm working as intended, not a cost.

My read: the reviewer's argument is correct and the middle option does not answer it, only the example. But reversing two shipped witnesses hours after they merged is a product call, so I am not taking it unilaterally.

## 3 — `exemptionIsVoid` enumerates link-creating verbs. LOWEST, and the most tempting to fix badly.

`LINK_CREATION = /\bln\s|\bsymlinkSync\b|\bos\.symlink\b|\bsymlink\s*\(/` plus a `commandWord === 'ln'` check. A list of ways to make a link is wrong the moment someone uses a way that is not on it. **Do not extend the regex.**

The reviewer's alternative makes the exemption provable at decision time: refuse unless the destination's whole directory chain already exists, forgiving only ancestors an earlier segment `mkdir`s via `createdAsDirectory`. That replaces "which verbs make links" with "is the destination's tree already real", which has no list. Unmeasured — whoever takes it should sweep it before believing the cost, and my guess is that it is expensive, because a fixture is usually written into a directory the same command just created.

---

Related: #1240 (interpreter heredocs, fixed), #1249 (the `segments()` backslash lookbehind, open and unclaimed), #1216 (none of this is running on the author's machine yet).

findings.title: audit-specs --fix rewrites a DERIVED spec that says 'do not edit here' on line 12, breaking the hash that pins it
findings.body:
Found on a real consumer (`pov-plugin`) during the `0.5.0 → 0.8.1` upgrade, 2026-10-22.

`bunx rungate audit-specs --fix` injected **39 lines** of `<!-- REVIEW: unmatched (...) -->` into `specs/POV-SPEC.md`. That file is generated by the consumer's own `scripts/sync-spec.ts` and hash-pinned by its `test/spec-drift.test.ts`. The edit:

1. broke the recorded `body-sha256`, reddening the consumer's suite
2. would have been **silently discarded** by the next `sync-spec.ts` run anyway

So the write is simultaneously destructive and futile. It was reverted by hand with `git checkout --`.

## Mechanism

`scripts/audit-specs.ts` has exactly one write site and no guard of any kind:

```
$ git grep -n "writeFileSync" origin/main -- scripts/audit-specs.ts
11:import { readFileSync, writeFileSync, readdirSync, existsSync } from "fs";
703:        writeFileSync(filePath, modified);
```

```ts
      if (hasChanges) {
        writeFileSync(filePath, modified);   // :703
      }
```

Spec discovery selects on `testable` and `compliance` in the frontmatter. Nothing asks whether the bytes are authored or produced.

## The file said so, in English, above the fold

```
 1  ---
 2  doc-type: spec
...
 9  compliance: strict
10  ---
11
12  <!-- DERIVED FILE — do not edit here.
13
14  The canonical POV spec lives in ... specs/pov-spec.md.
...  it is regenerated by `bun scripts/sync-spec.ts`, and
```

Line 12. `--fix` edited it on line 355. The marker is human-readable only, which is the actual gap — a consumer who does the right thing and labels a derived file gets no protection from it.

## Why this is not just "add a check"

`--fix` cannot know a file is generated unless generated files say so **machine-readably**, and today there are at least three conventions in play across consumers: a `generated-sha` frontmatter key (used by `.claude/rules/*`), a `<!-- DERIVED FILE -->` HTML comment (this consumer), and nothing at all. The repair worth having is one declared key that every write path in the scaffold consults, not a second special case in `audit-specs.ts`.

Note the asymmetry with the rules path, which already has the concept: `.claude/rules/key-files.md` carries `generated-sha:` and the scaffold honours it. `specs/` has no equivalent, so the most carefully-maintained spec in a consumer tree is the least protected file in it.

## Success criteria

- [ ] SC-1: a spec carrying the generated marker is NOT written by `--fix`; it is reported as skipped, naming the marker and the generator
- [ ] SC-2: proven by mutation — removing the guard makes the marked fixture get written, and the case goes red
- [ ] SC-3: negative control — an ordinary hand-authored spec with unmatched SCs IS still rewritten, so the guard cannot be satisfied by refusing everything
- [ ] SC-4: the marker is one declared key consulted by every scaffold write path, not a check local to `audit-specs.ts`
- [ ] SC-5: a derived spec that declares the marker only as prose (an HTML comment, as here) is reported as UNPROTECTED rather than silently treated as authored

findings.title: claimCovers is a second decider for underPrefix, and it disagrees fail-open on ./, case and backslash
findings.body:
`lib/file-claims.ts` ships `claimCovers`, which answers a question `lib/repo-path.ts`'s `underPrefix` already owns. Two deciders for one question is the fourth shape in `.claude/rules/checks-must-be-able-to-fail.md`: both are real code, both are called, both look covered, and no behavioural test can tell them apart — a mutation of either leaves the other holding the case up.

Filed as a follow-up rather than a review round, so #1436 could land green. It did: `483ce37c`.

## The current code

```ts
export function claimCovers(claimed: string, path: string): boolean {
  const c = claimed.replace(/\/+$/, "");
  return path === c || path.startsWith(`${c}/`);
}
```

## Measured disagreements

Against `underPrefix` from `lib/repo-path.ts` on main, for the claim `lib`:

| input | `claimCovers` | `underPrefix` | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `./lib/x.ts` | `false` | `true` | **disagree** |
| `Lib/x.ts` | `false` | `true` | **disagree** |
| `lib\x.ts` | `false` | `true` | **disagree** |
| `library/x.ts` | `false` | `false` | both correct |

All three disagreements fail in the same direction: **`claimCovers` says a path is not covered when it is.** For a lock, that is the fail-open side — it reports a claimed file as unclaimed, which is exactly the reading the guard exists to prevent. `./lib/x.ts` is not exotic; it is what a `git diff --name-only` pipe produces on some paths and what an agent writes by hand constantly.

## The fix

Delete `claimCovers` and call `underPrefix`. Not "make `claimCovers` match" — a second implementation that currently agrees is the defect, because the next normalisation added to one of them silently reopens the gap, and the test suite cannot see it.

## What to break to prove it

Point the call site at `underPrefix`, then feed `./lib/x.ts` through the `check` path of `scripts/claim-files.ts` with `lib` claimed by another owner. It must refuse. Under the old predicate it reports free.

## Which SUCCESS.md claim this moves

None directly — it is a correctness fix inside #1413's lock, so it protects the parallel-agent claim rather than advancing one. Cleanup, and it should say so rather than borrow urgency.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

findings.title: claimCovers is a second decider: a contended file reads FREE under ./lib, Lib and a backslash
findings.body:
Raised on #1436's review and merged without it, by agreement — the PR was green and this is a clean follow-up rather than a reason to hold it.

`lib/file-claims.ts` exports `claimCovers`, four lines of `startsWith` answering a question `lib/repo-path.ts` already centralises as `underPrefix`:

```ts
export function claimCovers(claimed: string, path: string): boolean {
  const c = claimed.replace(/\/+$/, "");
  return path === c || path.startsWith(`${c}/`);
}
```

Two deciders for one question — `.claude/rules/checks-must-be-able-to-fail.md`, *the fourth shape*. They disagree on exactly the inputs a caller produces by accident.

### Measured, for the claim `lib`

| path | `claimCovers` | `underPrefix` |
|---|---|---|
| `./lib/x.ts` | false | **true** |
| `Lib/x.ts` | false | **true** |
| `lib\x.ts` | false | **true** |
| `lib/x.ts` | true | true |
| `library/x.ts` | false | false |
| `../lib/x.ts` | false | false |

Three contended paths read **FREE**. `./lib/...` is what tab-completion produces, the case variant is what a case-insensitive filesystem produces, and the backslash is what a Windows-shaped tool produces.

The registry side is already safe — `claimFault` rejects absolute and `..` entries — so this is specifically the **caller-supplied** path, which nothing normalises. That asymmetry is why it is not visible from the registry fixtures.

### Why the suite could not see it

Every fixture in `test/file-claims.test.ts`'s coverage table is already normalised, because that is how anybody writes a fixture by hand. A rule that normalises and a rule that does not agree on all of them. The test population and the defect sit on different axes — the *seventh shape*.

### The fix

One import and a delegation. `underPrefix` is strictly better here: segment-aware (`library/x.ts` still does not match `lib`) and it refuses a `..` that leaves the repository, so it is tighter where it matters and looser only where the local rule was wrong.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC-1 — `claimCovers` delegates to `underPrefix`; no second normalisation rule remains in `lib/file-claims.ts`
- [ ] AC-2 — the coverage table gains the adversarial rows (`./`, case, backslash, leading slash) that the hand-written fixtures could not reach
- [ ] AC-3 — an assertion binds the delegation over the adversarial set, so reintroducing a local rule is red rather than silently equivalent
- [ ] AC-4 — rows that cannot discriminate between the two rules are labelled as documentation rather than counted as witnesses

### Claim this moves

**Claim 1 — gates can fail.** A contended file reported FREE is the file-claim mechanism failing silently in the direction it exists to prevent, and the existing table could not have caught it.
